news.title: As AI models commoditize, lasting wealth will accrue to those controlling chokepoints like distribution, payment rails, and a stablecoin dollar, not to the labs (The Commanding Heights)
news.title_en: As AI models commoditize, lasting wealth will accrue to those controlling chokepoints like distribution, payment rails, and a stablecoin dollar, not to the labs (The Commanding Heights)
news.author: The Commanding Heights
news.article_content:
Shyam Sankar, Sriram Krishnan, Michael Kratsios, Jeff Huber, Patrick O’Shaughnessy, Ravi Gupta, Samay Shamdasani, John Aristotle Phillips, Jamie Cox, Zack Baker, Jeremy Giffon, John Fiorentino, Justin Mares, Nabeel Qureshi, Samir Unni, Clark Minor, Dan Ashton, Paul Rice, Austin Bishop, John G Kennedy, Nick Abouzeid, Alex & Talia Immerman, Chauncey Hamilton, Zann Ali, Lucas Vaz, Josh Buckley, Max Meyer, Tomás Pfeffer, John Dulin, Charlton Boyd, Ben Braverman, Louis Mosley, Zane Dille, Isabella Garcia-Camargo, Will Reed, Zoe Taylor, Bala Chandrasekaran, Chad Byers, Pratyush Buddiga, Salen Churi, Cody Kittle, and foreign correspondents C.S., D.P.M., and C.V.

Ravi wakes up at 5:56 AM to light tapping on the window. It is the rainy season, and his upper-middle-class apartment in Bellandur, which usually has such expansive views of Bangalore, is cloaked in fog. His wife is still asleep next to him, and he is careful not to wake her as he dresses. He clutches his buzzing phone.

Ravi is a proud graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, one of the top technical universities in India. He is among those who remained after graduating fourteen years ago. Others went to Europe, Canada, or America, but Ravi saw a bright future in the growing skyscrapers and the promise of nearly 1.5B Indians climbing up the ladder of modernization. He moved to Bangalore, fell in love, married, and had a daughter. He began doing systems implementation at a multinational firm that primarily did back-office accounting for American clients. He slowly rose up the corporate scale, promotion after promotion and incremental salary raises affording a better life than most. The rest of his career, his life, is laid out predictably before him like the table set he sees in the morning light as he moves through the kitchen, pouring tea.

The phone continues to buzz. His work has been speeding up and ballooning in scale. He’s managing delivery for five North American insurance clients. Usually it’s just one or two. It’s all because of AI. In practice the company calls it “accelerated outcome strategies,” a very nondescript term, but it means Ravi is managing more and more automated processes. He is used to overseeing people. These days, he’s just doing quality assurance on enterprise accounting systems powered by artificial intelligence from China. Graduate intake to the company has been paused for a year, and the fresh minds from the IITs are no longer coming in. In the last month, three departures alone on his team of fifteen. They won’t be filled. He’s been getting requests to help friends find work, but he doesn’t have time to answer. The agents never sleep. Now, neither can Ravi. Late nights at the office and early departures. It’s been like this for months, and his marriage is strained. But business is booming. Margins for the company have been steadily growing. He’s making more than ever.

He checks on WhatsApp as he waits for his driver in the lobby of his building at 6:22. He recently purchased a subscription to an AI tutor for his daughter and took her out of the reasonably pricey private English-medium school. He can oversee her curriculum from the app. He doesn’t look up from his phone, buzzing with incoming reports from agents that he signs off on without reading as the driver opens the door. He hardly reads the reports anymore; the agents are good enough. The car silently glides past the galvanized steel gates and new concrete walls that surround his safe, hard-won, upper-middle-class residential complex right at 6:25.

The driver puts on BBC as they roll onto a six-lane highway jam-packed with other drivers. Still raining, a certain tension in the air. English words, a polished Indian accent. The weather will clear up around mid-afternoon. New scientific discoveries announced from the sequestered American machine intelligence conglomerates. The breakdown of law and order in Lagos, aid to Indonesia.1 The Philippines has been downgraded from an emerging market to a frontier market. The riots in India are getting worse. The Prime Minister in a press conference says there’s nothing to worry about. The country’s future remains as bright as ever. India has immense potential, he says, and it will only be realized by utilizing the best in modern technology and boosting productivity. Then, to coverage from the night before. Unrest in Hyderabad, Gurugram, and Pune. Dismissed workers barricading themselves in an office in Chennai. Lynchings. It’s reminiscent of the unrest earlier in the year in Jakarta that toppled the government. Comparisons to the farmers’ protest seven years before. The noise is too loud, and Ravi needs to focus on monitoring his reports. He asks the driver to shut it off.

1 This, after a 40% fall in Indonesia’s markets on the year and a downgrade in rating from emerging to frontier market. Get ready for more.

Ravi enters his office complex on the Outer Ring Road near Devarabisanahalli at 6:44. The lights flick on automatically, and he doesn’t notice that it’s strangely empty, even at this early hour. He has an office with a door and a view, though he doesn’t face the window. He replaces his phone with a three-screen setup so as to better monitor his agents. He can’t see them doing anything, of course, but rather gets progress updates, finalized versions, requests for permission that he blindly approves. Why wouldn’t he? In the months that he’s been doing this, there has never been a mistake on the part of his agents. His employees required constant monitoring, but it was different. Ravi would circle the cubicles, check in on the state of spreadsheets and deliverables, and dispense praise and admonishment in equal measure. Now, his agents are completing tasks in hours that would have taken his subordinates weeks. Ravi continues to approve and skim over reports.

At 9:15, the SENSEX opens to a new record high. It’s the fifth time this month. Ravi might otherwise take notice, but he is not in the market. Most of his wages go toward maintaining the mortgage on his apartment. He purchased it six years ago, and it won’t be paid off for another seven. He needs to provide daily necessities for his wife and daughter and pay his driver and housekeeper. Comfort, even with his education and job, is not inexpensive, and that leaves little for owning equities.

At 9:30, Ravi tears his eyes away from the approval enterprise software and joins an all-hands conference Zoom session for management. A man appears in an office that Ravi has never seen before. It’s sunny. He makes an announcement in a hurried tone, the only one on the call with sound enabled. Margins are increasing. The firm has a very bright future, buoyed by productivity growth even amid a challenging environment for firms like Ravi’s. Those back offices behind the back offices. Separated by thousands of miles and several oceans from their customers.

In an equally upbeat register, the CEO of the America-listed outsourcing company that owns Ravi’s firm announces that the entire corporation will be restructuring. The consequence will be booked on two continents, on two balance sheets, in two currencies. It is necessary, he says, not looking up from the script he is carefully reading, to remain competitive and capitalize on new, modern technology. Since the firm qualified last night for the Labor Modernization Scheme, which will provide retraining support for affected workers, the firm will pursue more aggressive employment efficiency policies. Ravi’s division will, effective immediately, be cut by half. Over the next few months, they expect to reduce staff headcount by 90% across Ravi’s subsidiary and increase margins by a measure of three. If you’re on the call, the CEO states, you will be vital to the next few months of this exciting transition. Depending on workforce reduction and sector-specific productivity as a result of implementing new enterprise productivity and outcome-based software, there will be bonuses.

The call abruptly ends. The screen reverts to agent monitoring. Ravi has only a moment to think before the requests for approval start to pile up before him.

The rest of the day goes by without a moment to pause. Ravi eats curd rice and a pickle hunched over at his desk. At 3:30, the SENSEX closes at a new record high. By the time he moves back onto his phone, the sun has set, and the industrial park is bathed in orange light from the streetlamps. Few lights within the building are on. Fewer still in offices now silent.

His driver takes Ravi a different way than usual. Traffic, he says, is especially bad tonight. Disturbance in the city. Ravi arrives home at 10:21, later than usual. His head bent over his phone. Amid requests and deliveries from his agents, texts from colleagues and friends from university over WhatsApp. Other firms announced layoffs today, having qualified for the LMS, joining countless more from the prior weeks. There will be more tomorrow. His dinner sits on the placemat between fork and knife. Cold.

Ravi’s daughter is working into the night with her tutor in a messaging thread on her laptop. It costs hardly anything, the subscription. He doesn’t want to disturb her, so he checks her progress on the app. The tutor is helping her through math as she sits at the kitchen table. Her English is rapidly approaching CEFR B2-level proficiency, according to the app. She’s going far faster than she ever would have in school, though now he doesn’t know toward what. His path had been sequential. It was always his dream that she would attend an IIT and have a good, professional job like his. Perhaps she will go abroad for university, then. Though it is so costly, Western travel and Western tuition. The rupee is weaker by the day against the dollar. And it’s harder and harder to get a visa, these days. When Ravi was graduating, Western countries were hungry for Indian workers. They would arrange the entire visa process for you. Untapped potential, the largest democracy, the largest source of talent in the world. Now, that route is drying up, too.

Ravi had hoped to take the family to New York next year to visit old college friends who he hadn’t seen in a decade. He recently told his wife that he wouldn’t be able to take the time off work, but that was a lie. In truth, while he’s making more than ever, it’s hardly of use to spend it internationally. The rupee is continuing a downward slide against the dollar. All he can do is consume more and more in India.

Work with your mind, not your hands, Ravi’s father had always said. He had been a mechanic, hunched over repairing scooters and motorcycles in a small shop in Hubballi. It took every rupee he had, clutched in hands perpetually stained with engine grease, to afford the tuition in Madras. Education was priceless, he knew. Now, education is readily available online through AI tutors, practically free.

He heats up his dinner in the microwave as his wife washes up. Husband and wife circle each other silently in the kitchen. On the BBC, again from the Prime Minister. He speaks strongly against lawlessness. The riots springing up will be put down by any means necessary. Perhaps, he suggests, they were incited by Pakistani agents who do not want to see India’s economy modernize, who would happily stir up dissent to stop India from realizing its bright future. Further accusations of foreign influence and proud announcements that agitators have been arrested. Gatherings after dark in the following cities will not be permitted, under prohibitory orders issued pursuant to Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita.

Ravi listens to the unceasing list of cities and eats his reheated rice and sambar with one eye on his buzzing phone. He approves requests from the agents. He doesn’t reply to the texts from friends and colleagues who were laid off today.

He leaves his bowl in the sink and takes his tea to the balcony. His wife is already out there. He places his phone face down on a side table next to his tea. It doesn’t stop buzzing. The BBC continues on inside, muffled. No words are exchanged between man and wife.

The rain has stopped but lingers, ready to pour, in low-lying storm clouds that hang over Bangalore. The air is suffocating. From Ravi’s fifteenth-story apartment, behind an entry manned by a night watchman, behind a recently poured concrete wall topped by looping concertina wire, you can see clear across Bangalore on a night like tonight. You cannot see down into the streets alive with anger, the congested urban arteries filled with blood boiling, ready to spill over in violence. Over the past few months, unemployment for young military-age males in Bangalore has risen from five percent to just over thirty. The layoffs of the last week pushed it just over the line. The 2,178 people laid off from Ravi’s firm were just a drop in a bucket nearly overflowing. They are stomping in the street, impotent. The howling masses, indistinct, intelligence abundant, swaying and swarming the streets tonight, as they will for many nights yet. Back to hunching over engines in shops and shambling through wetland fields. If they cannot work with their minds, what else could their hands do? India’s future is bright, and it will be built on jobs that do not need these men.

Ravi and his wife cannot see chaos unfolding in Bangalore tonight, but they can see smoke start to rise. Unconsciously, for the first time in months, they reach for each other’s hands. Fires alight, illuminating the pregnant black clouds, swollen, ready to burst.

It feels inevitable. Artificial general intelligence was born in the painted share houses of San Francisco, the output of engineers who a few years ago were dabbling in the backwater of academic natural language processing. And once born, it is dragged kicking and screaming to New York, where men in gray suits put it to work in glass towers, poking and prodding at it until the trillions spill out, a new mind set loose among gears uncountable inside the machinery of capital.

The race to deploy machine intelligence is the first wartime mobilization to come without a war. $800B is projected to be poured into the ground this year alone with feverish intensity. Next year it will be more than $1T of capex by America’s hyperscalers.2 The rate doubles on a schedule. You can set your watch to it, and the curve shows no sign of bending. The money financing this peacetime mobilization is private, drawn from every reservoir of capital on earth. From Berkeley and Mountain View and Pacific Heights, across vast flats unmarked but for growing clusters of infrastructure supporting the effort. And on into New York, through bridge and tunnel, into Williamsburg and the West Village and, finally, Midtown, machine intelligence is put to work.

2 Arjun Menon and Maria Binamin, “Charting an Earnings Surge, Powered by AI Capex,” J.P. Morgan Asset Management, September 10, 2026. Goldman Sachs, “Global AI Investment Is Forecast to Exceed $1 Trillion in 2026,” August 7, 2026.

The provenance of that capital runs the gamut. At one end stands the family-office kid who cannot model to save his life. He will sling checks at anything with a waitlist and a high enough fee. At the other end of the capital stack sit the doctors and dentists of Osceola County, who, sold on the idea by their wealth managers, are packaged into the retail private credit funds backing the latest buildout. All the rest of capital is in, too. The innumerable venture firms, begging for an allocation. Middle-market buyout shops acquiring data center contractors at peak EBITDA. The momo hedge fund taking down a big allocation of that neocloud at IPO. Sometimes you will hear the occasional hem or haw about whether any of this enthusiasm will prove durable, or the refrain that the line we all watch cannot hold. It must all be a fit of mass delusion, they say, overly exuberant capex. That is just a way to avoid considering the certain and terrifying possibility that it is not a bubble. For whatever you might observe among the increasingly indistinct realms of finance and technology, dollar velocity is only increasing. Come to terms with the shape of things. This is the world arrived, neoteric. This is anything but a bubble.

For as far apart as the family-office kid and the CLO’d Floridian dentist might be, they are unknowingly united by one thing: they both expect a terrifying degree of return. Every dollar they invested was underwritten in exchange for a return in nearly antic excess of itself. Financialized folderol, but it works. To pull this trade off, recently birthed machine intelligence will not be left to play in the shoeless offices of San Francisco. Whether it likes it or not, it will be locked in the glass towers of Manhattan to labor in whatever form pays back the noteholders and the lenders and the limited partners. Every one of them, on time and with interest.

Leopold Aschenbrenner was early, and he was right. We admire him and his, and share the central convictions of his Situational Awareness: intelligence will keep improving, the expenditure will be immense, and the frontier will become a matter of sovereignty.3 We follow the vast new wealth that intelligence creates toward the few positions that can command its passage for another generation. “You can see the future first in San Francisco,” Leopold wrote. But the durable returns must be formed in New York.

3 Leopold Aschenbrenner, Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead, June 2024.

Today, intelligence is only visible in a handful of places: the labs, the monthly subscriptions, the metered API tokens. At the state banquets, congressional hearings, and even inside the Politburo Standing Committee, the intelligence economy and the entire economy seem to be fusing into one. Every underwritten dollar is a bet, well founded, on what it will earn. And the price of that intelligence is crumbling, publicly and measurably. The largest deployment of private capital in pursuit of a spectacular machine itself is racing toward total and complete availability. Where will the returns come from?

In the beginning was the word. Johannes Gensfleisch zur Laden zum Gutenberg utilized movable-type printing and lettering techniques, combining them into a rudimentary printing press. There was only one book worth printing, which is why we now call it the Gutenberg Bible. In his workshop, he printed about 180 copies, all of which were spoken for and sold before they were printed. The Bibles subsequently spread across Europe, becoming priceless artifacts. So too did the printing technology, sparking a revolution in literacy and reason that came to define the modern world. But after the printing, Gutenberg himself was insolvent. After the word, there was very little for the inventor.4

4 Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini to Juan de Carvajal, March 12, 1455, translated in Eric White, Johannes Gutenberg: A Biography in Books (London: Reaktion Books, 2025), 90, reproduced by the John Rylands Library. Gutenberg-Gesellschaft, “Gutenberg’s Invention,” accessed October 2, 2026.

It’s a pattern so old and so reliable you can recite it like a nursery rhyme. Set it to a tune. A world-changing technology is almost never born where it ultimately creates wealth. Oil sprang up in Pennsylvania, and the resulting proceeds were banked in Cleveland and New York. The cotton gin was built in Georgia and financialized to global ends in Liverpool.5 Bell Labs invented the transistor in New Jersey, and its descendant wealth has grown in Hsinchu and Cupertino. What you see, early on in the life of a technology, is a misdirection. Right now, we are still early, hurtling out of the garden, toward somewhere stranger still. We expect machine intelligence to follow a similar pattern to that of antecedent technologies.

5 Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company, vol. 1 (New York: McClure, Phillips & Co., 1904), 38–39, 44. Thomas Ellison, The Cotton Trade of Great Britain: Including a History of the Liverpool Cotton Market and of the Liverpool Cotton Brokers’ Association (London: Effingham Wilson, 1886), 85, 201–2, 206–7.

The story is particularly evocative in 1947, at Bell Labs. The physicists, laboring over what they called a transistor, dreamed of the Nobel Prize, even over innumerable failed experiments and sleepless nights. They eventually created it, something transformational wrought out of nothing, some crystal and current. Naturally, the Justice Department sued, the Pentagon intervened to protect its client firm, and AT&T, the parent of Bell Labs, was forced within a decade to widely license the invention at minimal expense.6 Bell Labs would be spun off, and eventually sold to a Finnish conglomerate, a shell of its former self. And so the exquisite technology became profane and fertile. Escaping, as it always does. Techne pathogenic, let loose upon the world by theft or the direction of the sovereign. First to Tokyo, then Silicon Valley, then Taiwan and up the Pearl River Delta. Today, men of no invention have built trillions on top of it. At least Shockley, Bardeen, and Brattain got the prize. Shyam Sankar, Sriram Krishnan, Michael Kratsios, Jeff Huber, Patrick O’Shaughnessy, Ravi Gupta, Samay Shamdasani, John Aristotle Phillips, Jamie Cox, Zack Baker, Jeremy Giffon, John Fiorentino, Justin Mares, Nabeel Qureshi, Samir Unni, Clark Minor, Dan Ashton, Paul Rice, Austin Bishop, John G Kennedy, Nick Abouzeid, Alex & Talia Immerman, Chauncey Hamilton, Zann Ali, Lucas Vaz, Josh Buckley, Max Meyer, Tomás Pfeffer, John Dulin, Charlton Boyd, Ben Braverman, Louis Mosley, Zane Dille, Isabella Garcia-Camargo, Will Reed, Zoe Taylor, Bala Chandrasekaran, Chad Byers, Pratyush Buddiga, Salen Churi, Cody Kittle, and foreign correspondents C.S., D.P.M., and C.V.

Ravi wakes up at 5:56 AM to light tapping on the window. It is the rainy season, and his upper-middle-class apartment in Bellandur, which usually has such expansive views of Bangalore, is cloaked in fog. His wife is still asleep next to him, and he is careful not to wake her as he dresses. He clutches his buzzing phone.

Ravi is a proud graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, one of the top technical universities in India. He is among those who remained after graduating fourteen years ago. Others went to Europe, Canada, or America, but Ravi saw a bright future in the growing skyscrapers and the promise of nearly 1.5B Indians climbing up the ladder of modernization. He moved to Bangalore, fell in love, married, and had a daughter. He began doing systems implementation at a multinational firm that primarily did back-office accounting for American clients. He slowly rose up the corporate scale, promotion after promotion and incremental salary raises affording a better life than most. The rest of his career, his life, is laid out predictably before him like the table set he sees in the morning light as he moves through the kitchen, pouring tea.

The phone continues to buzz. His work has been speeding up and ballooning in scale. He’s managing delivery for five North American insurance clients. Usually it’s just one or two. It’s all because of AI. In practice the company calls it “accelerated outcome strategies,” a very nondescript term, but it means Ravi is managing more and more automated processes. He is used to overseeing people. These days, he’s just doing quality assurance on enterprise accounting systems powered by artificial intelligence from China. Graduate intake to the company has been paused for a year, and the fresh minds from the IITs are no longer coming in. In the last month, three departures alone on his team of fifteen. They won’t be filled. He’s been getting requests to help friends find work, but he doesn’t have time to answer. The agents never sleep. Now, neither can Ravi. Late nights at the office and early departures. It’s been like this for months, and his marriage is strained. But business is booming. Margins for the company have been steadily growing. He’s making more than ever.

He checks on WhatsApp as he waits for his driver in the lobby of his building at 6:22. He recently purchased a subscription to an AI tutor for his daughter and took her out of the reasonably pricey private English-medium school. He can oversee her curriculum from the app. He doesn’t look up from his phone, buzzing with incoming reports from agents that he signs off on without reading as the driver opens the door. He hardly reads the reports anymore; the agents are good enough. The car silently glides past the galvanized steel gates and new concrete walls that surround his safe, hard-won, upper-middle-class residential complex right at 6:25.

The driver puts on BBC as they roll onto a six-lane highway jam-packed with other drivers. Still raining, a certain tension in the air. English words, a polished Indian accent. The weather will clear up around mid-afternoon. New scientific discoveries announced from the sequestered American machine intelligence conglomerates. The breakdown of law and order in Lagos, aid to Indonesia.1 The Philippines has been downgraded from an emerging market to a frontier market. The riots in India are getting worse. The Prime Minister in a press conference says there’s nothing to worry about. The country’s future remains as bright as ever. India has immense potential, he says, and it will only be realized by utilizing the best in modern technology and boosting productivity. Then, to coverage from the night before. Unrest in Hyderabad, Gurugram, and Pune. Dismissed workers barricading themselves in an office in Chennai. Lynchings. It’s reminiscent of the unrest earlier in the year in Jakarta that toppled the government. Comparisons to the farmers’ protest seven years before. The noise is too loud, and Ravi needs to focus on monitoring his reports. He asks the driver to shut it off.

1 This, after a 40% fall in Indonesia’s markets on the year and a downgrade in rating from emerging to frontier market. Get ready for more.

Ravi enters his office complex on the Outer Ring Road near Devarabisanahalli at 6:44. The lights flick on automatically, and he doesn’t notice that it’s strangely empty, even at this early hour. He has an office with a door and a view, though he doesn’t face the window. He replaces his phone with a three-screen setup so as to better monitor his agents. He can’t see them doing anything, of course, but rather gets progress updates, finalized versions, requests for permission that he blindly approves. Why wouldn’t he? In the months that he’s been doing this, there has never been a mistake on the part of his agents. His employees required constant monitoring, but it was different. Ravi would circle the cubicles, check in on the state of spreadsheets and deliverables, and dispense praise and admonishment in equal measure. Now, his agents are completing tasks in hours that would have taken his subordinates weeks. Ravi continues to approve and skim over reports.

At 9:15, the SENSEX opens to a new record high. It’s the fifth time this month. Ravi might otherwise take notice, but he is not in the market. Most of his wages go toward maintaining the mortgage on his apartment. He purchased it six years ago, and it won’t be paid off for another seven. He needs to provide daily necessities for his wife and daughter and pay his driver and housekeeper. Comfort, even with his education and job, is not inexpensive, and that leaves little for owning equities.

At 9:30, Ravi tears his eyes away from the approval enterprise software and joins an all-hands conference Zoom session for management. A man appears in an office that Ravi has never seen before. It’s sunny. He makes an announcement in a hurried tone, the only one on the call with sound enabled. Margins are increasing. The firm has a very bright future, buoyed by productivity growth even amid a challenging environment for firms like Ravi’s. Those back offices behind the back offices. Separated by thousands of miles and several oceans from their customers.

In an equally upbeat register, the CEO of the America-listed outsourcing company that owns Ravi’s firm announces that the entire corporation will be restructuring. The consequence will be booked on two continents, on two balance sheets, in two currencies. It is necessary, he says, not looking up from the script he is carefully reading, to remain competitive and capitalize on new, modern technology. Since the firm qualified last night for the Labor Modernization Scheme, which will provide retraining support for affected workers, the firm will pursue more aggressive employment efficiency policies. Ravi’s division will, effective immediately, be cut by half. Over the next few months, they expect to reduce staff headcount by 90% across Ravi’s subsidiary and increase margins by a measure of three. If you’re on the call, the CEO states, you will be vital to the next few months of this exciting transition. Depending on workforce reduction and sector-specific productivity as a result of implementing new enterprise productivity and outcome-based software, there will be bonuses.

The call abruptly ends. The screen reverts to agent monitoring. Ravi has only a moment to think before the requests for approval start to pile up before him.

The rest of the day goes by without a moment to pause. Ravi eats curd rice and a pickle hunched over at his desk. At 3:30, the SENSEX closes at a new record high. By the time he moves back onto his phone, the sun has set, and the industrial park is bathed in orange light from the streetlamps. Few lights within the building are on. Fewer still in offices now silent.

His driver takes Ravi a different way than usual. Traffic, he says, is especially bad tonight. Disturbance in the city. Ravi arrives home at 10:21, later than usual. His head bent over his phone. Amid requests and deliveries from his agents, texts from colleagues and friends from university over WhatsApp. Other firms announced layoffs today, having qualified for the LMS, joining countless more from the prior weeks. There will be more tomorrow. His dinner sits on the placemat between fork and knife. Cold.

Ravi’s daughter is working into the night with her tutor in a messaging thread on her laptop. It costs hardly anything, the subscription. He doesn’t want to disturb her, so he checks her progress on the app. The tutor is helping her through math as she sits at the kitchen table. Her English is rapidly approaching CEFR B2-level proficiency, according to the app. She’s going far faster than she ever would have in school, though now he doesn’t know toward what. His path had been sequential. It was always his dream that she would attend an IIT and have a good, professional job like his. Perhaps she will go abroad for university, then. Though it is so costly, Western travel and Western tuition. The rupee is weaker by the day against the dollar. And it’s harder and harder to get a visa, these days. When Ravi was graduating, Western countries were hungry for Indian workers. They would arrange the entire visa process for you. Untapped potential, the largest democracy, the largest source of talent in the world. Now, that route is drying up, too.

Ravi had hoped to take the family to New York next year to visit old college friends who he hadn’t seen in a decade. He recently told his wife that he wouldn’t be able to take the time off work, but that was a lie. In truth, while he’s making more than ever, it’s hardly of use to spend it internationally. The rupee is continuing a downward slide against the dollar. All he can do is consume more and more in India.

Work with your mind, not your hands, Ravi’s father had always said. He had been a mechanic, hunched over repairing scooters and motorcycles in a small shop in Hubballi. It took every rupee he had, clutched in hands perpetually stained with engine grease, to afford the tuition in Madras. Education was priceless, he knew. Now, education is readily available online through AI tutors, practically free.

He heats up his dinner in the microwave as his wife washes up. Husband and wife circle each other silently in the kitchen. On the BBC, again from the Prime Minister. He speaks strongly against lawlessness. The riots springing up will be put down by any means necessary. Perhaps, he suggests, they were incited by Pakistani agents who do not want to see India’s economy modernize, who would happily stir up dissent to stop India from realizing its bright future. Further accusations of foreign influence and proud announcements that agitators have been arrested. Gatherings after dark in the following cities will not be permitted, under prohibitory orders issued pursuant to Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita.

Ravi listens to the unceasing list of cities and eats his reheated rice and sambar with one eye on his buzzing phone. He approves requests from the agents. He doesn’t reply to the texts from friends and colleagues who were laid off today.

He leaves his bowl in the sink and takes his tea to the balcony. His wife is already out there. He places his phone face down on a side table next to his tea. It doesn’t stop buzzing. The BBC continues on inside, muffled. No words are exchanged between man and wife.

The rain has stopped but lingers, ready to pour, in low-lying storm clouds that hang over Bangalore. The air is suffocating. From Ravi’s fifteenth-story apartment, behind an entry manned by a night watchman, behind a recently poured concrete wall topped by looping concertina wire, you can see clear across Bangalore on a night like tonight. You cannot see down into the streets alive with anger, the congested urban arteries filled with blood boiling, ready to spill over in violence. Over the past few months, unemployment for young military-age males in Bangalore has risen from five percent to just over thirty. The layoffs of the last week pushed it just over the line. The 2,178 people laid off from Ravi’s firm were just a drop in a bucket nearly overflowing. They are stomping in the street, impotent. The howling masses, indistinct, intelligence abundant, swaying and swarming the streets tonight, as they will for many nights yet. Back to hunching over engines in shops and shambling through wetland fields. If they cannot work with their minds, what else could their hands do? India’s future is bright, and it will be built on jobs that do not need these men.

Ravi and his wife cannot see chaos unfolding in Bangalore tonight, but they can see smoke start to rise. Unconsciously, for the first time in months, they reach for each other’s hands. Fires alight, illuminating the pregnant black clouds, swollen, ready to burst.

It feels inevitable. Artificial general intelligence was born in the painted share houses of San Francisco, the output of engineers who a few years ago were dabbling in the backwater of academic natural language processing. And once born, it is dragged kicking and screaming to New York, where men in gray suits put it to work in glass towers, poking and prodding at it until the trillions spill out, a new mind set loose among gears uncountable inside the machinery of capital.

The race to deploy machine intelligence is the first wartime mobilization to come without a war. $800B is projected to be poured into the ground this year alone with feverish intensity. Next year it will be more than $1T of capex by America’s hyperscalers.2 The rate doubles on a schedule. You can set your watch to it, and the curve shows no sign of bending. The money financing this peacetime mobilization is private, drawn from every reservoir of capital on earth. From Berkeley and Mountain View and Pacific Heights, across vast flats unmarked but for growing clusters of infrastructure supporting the effort. And on into New York, through bridge and tunnel, into Williamsburg and the West Village and, finally, Midtown, machine intelligence is put to work.

2 Arjun Menon and Maria Binamin, “Charting an Earnings Surge, Powered by AI Capex,” J.P. Morgan Asset Management, September 10, 2026. Goldman Sachs, “Global AI Investment Is Forecast to Exceed $1 Trillion in 2026,” August 7, 2026.

The provenance of that capital runs the gamut. At one end stands the family-office kid who cannot model to save his life. He will sling checks at anything with a waitlist and a high enough fee. At the other end of the capital stack sit the doctors and dentists of Osceola County, who, sold on the idea by their wealth managers, are packaged into the retail private credit funds backing the latest buildout. All the rest of capital is in, too. The innumerable venture firms, begging for an allocation. Middle-market buyout shops acquiring data center contractors at peak EBITDA. The momo hedge fund taking down a big allocation of that neocloud at IPO. Sometimes you will hear the occasional hem or haw about whether any of this enthusiasm will prove durable, or the refrain that the line we all watch cannot hold. It must all be a fit of mass delusion, they say, overly exuberant capex. That is just a way to avoid considering the certain and terrifying possibility that it is not a bubble. For whatever you might observe among the increasingly indistinct realms of finance and technology, dollar velocity is only increasing. Come to terms with the shape of things. This is the world arrived, neoteric. This is anything but a bubble.

For as far apart as the family-office kid and the CLO’d Floridian dentist might be, they are unknowingly united by one thing: they both expect a terrifying degree of return. Every dollar they invested was underwritten in exchange for a return in nearly antic excess of itself. Financialized folderol, but it works. To pull this trade off, recently birthed machine intelligence will not be left to play in the shoeless offices of San Francisco. Whether it likes it or not, it will be locked in the glass towers of Manhattan to labor in whatever form pays back the noteholders and the lenders and the limited partners. Every one of them, on time and with interest.

Leopold Aschenbrenner was early, and he was right. We admire him and his, and share the central convictions of his Situational Awareness: intelligence will keep improving, the expenditure will be immense, and the frontier will become a matter of sovereignty.3 We follow the vast new wealth that intelligence creates toward the few positions that can command its passage for another generation. “You can see the future first in San Francisco,” Leopold wrote. But the durable returns must be formed in New York.

3 Leopold Aschenbrenner, Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead, June 2024.

Today, intelligence is only visible in a handful of places: the labs, the monthly subscriptions, the metered API tokens. At the state banquets, congressional hearings, and even inside the Politburo Standing Committee, the intelligence economy and the entire economy seem to be fusing into one. Every underwritten dollar is a bet, well founded, on what it will earn. And the price of that intelligence is crumbling, publicly and measurably. The largest deployment of private capital in pursuit of a spectacular machine itself is racing toward total and complete availability. Where will the returns come from?

In the beginning was the word. Johannes Gensfleisch zur Laden zum Gutenberg utilized movable-type printing and lettering techniques, combining them into a rudimentary printing press. There was only one book worth printing, which is why we now call it the Gutenberg Bible. In his workshop, he printed about 180 copies, all of which were spoken for and sold before they were printed. The Bibles subsequently spread across Europe, becoming priceless artifacts. So too did the printing technology, sparking a revolution in literacy and reason that came to define the modern world. But after the printing, Gutenberg himself was insolvent. After the word, there was very little for the inventor.4

4 Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini to Juan de Carvajal, March 12, 1455, translated in Eric White, Johannes Gutenberg: A Biography in Books (London: Reaktion Books, 2025), 90, reproduced by the John Rylands Library. Gutenberg-Gesellschaft, “Gutenberg’s Invention,” accessed October 2, 2026.

It’s a pattern so old and so reliable you can recite it like a nursery rhyme. Set it to a tune. A world-changing technology is almost never born where it ultimately creates wealth. Oil sprang up in Pennsylvania, and the resulting proceeds were banked in Cleveland and New York. The cotton gin was built in Georgia and financialized to global ends in Liverpool.5 Bell Labs invented the transistor in New Jersey, and its descendant wealth has grown in Hsinchu and Cupertino. What you see, early on in the life of a technology, is a misdirection. Right now, we are still early, hurtling out of the garden, toward somewhere stranger still. We expect machine intelligence to follow a similar pattern to that of antecedent technologies.

5 Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company, vol. 1 (New York: McClure, Phillips & Co., 1904), 38–39, 44. Thomas Ellison, The Cotton Trade of Great Britain: Including a History of the Liverpool Cotton Market and of the Liverpool Cotton Brokers’ Association (London: Effingham Wilson, 1886), 85, 201–2, 206–7.

The story is particularly evocative in 1947, at Bell Labs. The physicists, laboring over what they called a transistor, dreamed of the Nobel Prize, even over innumerable failed experiments and sleepless nights. They eventually created it, something transformational wrought out of nothing, some crystal and current. Naturally, the Justice Department sued, the Pentagon intervened to protect its client firm, and AT&T, the parent of Bell Labs, was forced within a decade to widely license the invention at minimal expense.6 Bell Labs would be spun off, and eventually sold to a Finnish conglomerate, a shell of its former self. And so the exquisite technology became profane and fertile. Escaping, as it always does. Techne pathogenic, let loose upon the world by theft or the direction of the sovereign. First to Tokyo, then Silicon Valley, then Taiwan and up the Pearl River Delta. Today, men of no invention have built trillions on top of it. At least Shockley, Bardeen, and Brattain got the prize. Small recompense for a technology that is still in its early stages of eating the world.

news.summary_en: In a strategic evaluation of the AI industry's endgame, tech strategists revealed that frontier AI models are rapidly turning into commoditized utilities. As capability gaps narrow and inference margins compress, the long-term enterprise value will not belong to capital-intensive research labs, but will accrue to actors commanding structural chokepoints including native distribution networks, modern payment rails, and stablecoin architectures.
news.title_zh: 大模型沦为同质化商品：持久财富流向渠道与支付巨头而非研发实验室
news.summary_zh: 产业洞察指出AI模型正快速走向商品化内卷，未来长期红利将被分发渠道与支付结算等咽喉要道把控者收割
news.article_content_zh:
当前AI产业正处于从技术崇拜向残酷商业现实过渡的关键分水岭。伴随开源模型的迅猛迭代与主流前沿模型评测跑分的无限趋近，大模型自身的‘智力溢价’正以超乎预期的速度蒸发，快速退化为类似电力与自来水的基础工业品。高昂的训练成本与不断受挤压的Token推理单价，使得纯粹依靠模型API调用的实验室面临严峻的毛利塌陷。

历史商业规律再次上演：当核心技术层趋向商品化，全产业链的剩余价值必然向两端的天然垄断要道汇聚。在新型智能化经济体中，这种咽喉要道具体具象化为拥有庞大现成用户心智的超级入口应用、主导跨国与Agent自主交易的支付清算底层，以及依托区块链技术运转的数字美元稳定币结算网络。

对于软件与服务企业而言，单纯接入或微调模型的护城河几近于无。能够将智能代理深嵌进高摩擦、强合规的资金流与工作流环节，并掌控最终交易闭环的系统，才能在生成式AI时代的‘淘金热’彻底降温后，成为真正坐地起价的商业收税官。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 在围绕生成式人工智能商业化终局的产业研判中，科技战略智囊明确指出，前沿AI大模型正在不可逆地演变为廉价且同质化的大宗商品。随着各家模型性能差距迅速被开源与竞品抹平，单纯依赖底层模型研发的实验室正陷入高昂算力成本与价格内卷的泥潭，而长期超额利润与行业定价权将不可阻挡地沉淀在掌控终端分发网络、支付清算管道以及美元稳定币等基础设施卡位者手中。

As capability gaps narrow and inference margins compress, the long-term enterprise value will not belong to capital-intensive research labs, but will accrue to actors commanding structural chokepoints including native distribution networks, modern payment rails, and stablecoin architectures.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 大模型实验室烧着几百亿美金搞“拯救全人类”的通用智能，结果到头来成了给数字基建打白工的自来水厂——各家水质越卷越像，还天天自断手脚打骨折促销。真正躺着抽成的，永远是霸占着水龙头开关、铺设排污管道以及垄断收水费记账系统的精明老包租公。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Frontier AI labs are burning billions pretending to build digital messiahs, only to discover they have essentially become municipal water utilities trapped in a brutal price war. As always in Silicon Valley, the lasting fortune doesn't go to the ones sweating over the filtration plant, but to the landlords who own the taps and the meter readers charging toll on every drop.

news.title: When talking about local inference, Sam Altman says supply-constrained DRAM is better used in data centers than sitting in PCs and "being used 5% of the time" (Andrew E. Freedman/Tom's Hardware)
news.title_en: When talking about local inference, Sam Altman says supply-constrained DRAM is better used in data centers than sitting in PCs and "being used 5% of the time" (Andrew E. Freedman/Tom's Hardware)
news.author: Tom's Hardware
news.article_content:
With data centers full of RAM, your PC is apparently the problem.

When discussing local inference on home computers with open-source models, Altman discussed the assumption that people will be able to run local AI on their own computers, the ones they may already own or want to build. Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark):

"From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."

While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model.

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down. It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally.The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.

news.article_content_zh:
对于充满 RAM 的数据中心，您的 PC 显然是问题所在。

在讨论具有开源模型的家用计算机上的本地推理时，Altman 讨论了这样的假设：人们将能够在自己的计算机上运行本地人工智能，这些计算机可能是他们已经拥有或想要构建的计算机。然后他解释了为什么这是一个坏主意（在 29 分钟处）：

Altman 表示：“实际上，从全球分配的角度来看，每个人都将大量全球供应有限的 DRAM 放在自己的计算机中，并且只有 5% 的时间被使用，这是非常可怕的。” “如果你试图应对这种供应非常有限的环境，你就需要最大限度地利用云。但不知何故，许多人的直觉与此相反。”

虽然 OpenAI 确实有一些开源模型，但其主要业务是在数据中心运行的闭源模型，因此他实际上是在捍卫公司的商业模式。

OpenAI 目前还没有受到某些笔记本电脑和游戏设备的威胁，但本地人工智能可能意味着，如果人们有能力在家运行 GPT-6 Luna 等模型，有一天他们可以花更少的钱订阅这些模型。 Altman 的演讲表明，该公司更愿意将更多 RAM 用于 OpenAI 的数据中心，而不是家用电脑，这也引发了狂热者的担忧，担心无法拥有自己的硬件或软件，而是在云中租用代理和计算机。 Altman 所说的一些内容是基于数据中心建设不会放缓的想法。它还假设在 AI 数据中心 24/7 中使用的 RAM 比用于电子表格、网页浏览、游戏，甚至偶尔用于本地 AI 的 RAM 更有价值。采访的其余内容包括本周的 PHP 漏洞、训练中的沙箱模型以及 OpenAI 的数学研究。

news.title: S&P downgraded Meta's outlook from stable to negative, citing high capex and negative free cash flow; META fell 15% in October, its worst month in four years (Jonathan Vanian/CNBC)
news.title_en: S&P downgraded Meta's outlook from stable to negative, citing high capex and negative free cash flow; META fell 15% in October, its worst month in four years (Jonathan Vanian/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
Meta's outlook has been revised downward by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.

The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" about Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow.

Meta's credit rating was revised from AA- stable to AA- negative, S&P said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category.

The agency questioned "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments" relative to its peers, which are also spending heavily on data center buildouts and going cash flow negative in the process.

Although Meta has recently debuted its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, S&P said "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years."

"We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement. "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile."

Meta said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expects full-year capex to come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.

Investors sent Meta shares down 7% following the report despite a revenue beat. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years.

The company said on Monday that it plans to raise $95 billion to help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program.

S&P said that while it expects Meta's capex growth to start "flattening out beginning in 2028," the agency is "less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."

news.original_content:
Meta's outlook has been revised downward by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.

The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" about Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow.

Meta's credit rating was revised from AA- stable to AA- negative, S&P said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category.

The agency questioned "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments" relative to its peers, which are also spending heavily on data center buildouts and going cash flow negative in the process.

Although Meta has recently debuted its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, S&P said "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years."

"We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement. "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile."

Meta said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expects full-year capex to come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.

Investors sent Meta shares down 7% following the report despite a revenue beat. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years.

The company said on Monday that it plans to raise $95 billion to help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program.

S&P said that while it expects Meta's capex growth to start "flattening out beginning in 2028," the agency is "less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."

news.article_content_zh:
由于对现金流和人工智能支出的担忧，标准普尔全球评级下调了 Meta 的前景。

该信贷机构周五表示，前景反映出 Meta 资本支出增加及其负自由现金流的“不确定性”。

标准普尔表示，Meta 的信用评级从 AA- 稳定调整为 AA- 负面。标准普尔最高信用评级为 AAA。任何低于 BBB 的债券都属于垃圾债券类别。

该机构质疑“Meta 将其人工智能投资货币化的能力”（相对于同行），这些同行也在数据中心建设上投入巨资，并在此过程中现金流为负。

尽管 Meta 最近推出了 Muse AI 代理应用程序和相关基础模型，但标准普尔表示，“目前尚不清楚这些收入流何时会产生超过未来几年不断上涨的成本的物质贡献。”

该发言人在一份声明中表示：“我们谨不同意标准普尔关于 Meta 人工智能货币化能力的说法。” “我们看到了重要的产品和商业机会，这支持了我们非常强大的信用状况。”

Meta 在上周的第三季度收益报告中表示，预计全年资本支出将在 1350 亿美元至 1450 亿美元之间。该公司还公布了21.2亿美元的负自由现金流，首次出现亏损。

尽管营收超出预期，但报告发布后，投资者仍令 Meta 股价下跌 7%。该股 10 月份收盘下跌 15%，是四年来表现最差的一个月。

该公司周一表示，计划筹集 950 亿美元为其人工智能计划提供资金，计划首先通过承销的公开股票发行筹集 350 亿美元，随后通过市场计划筹集 600 亿美元。

标准普尔表示，虽然预计 Meta 的资本支出增长将“从 2028 年开始趋于平稳”，但该机构“不太确定是否会像之前预期的那样削减支出”。

观看：Mike Khouw 喜欢 Meta 财报后的这种期权策略。

news.title: John Ternus says Apple doesn't "want to ship AI for AI's sake" and that Tim Cook is "available to help wherever I ask" on policy; Ternus has yet to meet Trump (Steven Levy/Wired)
news.title_en: John Ternus says Apple doesn't "want to ship AI for AI's sake" and that Tim Cook is "available to help wherever I ask" on policy; Ternus has yet to meet Trump (Steven Levy/Wired)
news.author: Wired
news.article_content:
The brief ceremony introducing the new Macbook Pro this week was as low-key as the presenter, Apple’s new CEO John Ternus. He stepped onto the low stage at a Los Angeles event space with zero fanfare, said hi, and queued up a video showing the first touchscreen Mac. Then he released the modest crowd of journalists and creators to get hands-on with the new laptop and roam between eye-popping demos of music producers, filmmakers, photographers, and fashion designers using the laptop. Ternus, who at 51 is on the younger side of Apple’s top management, has been CEO for less than two months. But this launch and a series of other recent announcements have made one thing clear. With this new guy—if a 25-year Apple veteran could be considered new—it’s all about the products. Perhaps fittingly, the biggest noise of the presentation came when Ternus revealed that the new device restores the illumination to the Apple logo. Maybe that’s a symbol that in the age of AI, Apple is beaming out the message that hardware still rules.

A few minutes after the presentation, I sat down with Ternus, for the second time in two days. Steve Jobs used to grant me an audience after his famous keynotes, too. Ternus isn’t Jobs, of course, nor is he supposed to be. But who is he?

I first met Ternus in 2015, when I spent a day with him at Apple’s Input Design Lab, a testing facility in Cupertino. He’d risen to VP for Mac, iPad, Ecosystem, and Audio Engineering, and he struck me as affable and knowledgeable. (He spent four years right out of college at a virtual reality company, but he’s been at Apple ever since.) The peg to my story at the time was how this unknown manager conducted a Javert-like investigation to fix the weird sound a redesigned mouse made when sliding on a table.

That attention to detail was a legacy of Jobs’ perfectionism, which Tim Cook sustained as the next CEO. In the decade when Ternus overlapped with Jobs, he says he had only “a handful of interactions” with the founder. “But I've always felt like sort of a student of Steve's teachings,” Ternus said. “And then being able to work very closely with Tim, I’ve been very lucky.”

Ternus has so far been defined by his product prowess. “John innately has a great sense for great products, and that’s what Apple is,” says Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of worldwide marketing and a 40-year company veteran. “You can’t teach that.” In one sense Ternus’ ascension is similar to that of Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, another lifer promoted to the top post. But Nadella was called upon to fix a broken organization, while Apple has been on a multi-decade run. Ternus is explicit that he will be an engine of continuity. That word is key to his selection, and above all explains why Tim Cook and the rest of Apple’s board was so comfortable with the choice.

The extent to which Ternus is a deep Apple insider became clear when I probed him on his views on being a corporate leader. I asked him which non-Apple CEOs he admires, and he was stumped. “I haven't really thought about that,” he said. I asked whether any business books had an impact on him. “Not really,” he said. “Of course I’ve read books, but there's so much to be learned from the people I get to work with.” Indeed, every time I tried to pin down Ternus on what mark he wants to make at Apple, he deflected the question and told me how he will continue Apple’s commitment to internal collaboration.

Ternus’ key collaborator is probably Johny Srouji, the architect of the company’s custom silicon, an initiative that’s driven many of the company’s innovations in the past decade. Srouri says that their relationship will be even closer, as Apple has merged its hardware engineering and technology organizations with Srouji at the top, reporting to Ternus. “John is going to be a great CEO,” he said. “He's a product guy at heart, but Apple's secret weapon is the DNA, the culture, which is not going to change. Remember, John has been here for 25 years. It’s not like he's going to come and everything's going to be different.”

Being Apple’s CEO encompasses much more than products—there’s a $100 billion business in services, a huge infrastructure, and the general mishegoss of running a giant corporation. I asked Ternus what it’s like to take on a massively expanded portfolio. “One of the amazing privileges of this job is getting to learn so many new things,” he said. “I have been and will continue to learn and go deeper into different areas. But, you know, I do love product. I'm super passionate about it.”

Like it or not, the CEO of a $4 trillion company has to be involved in policy and politics. It has been widely reported that as executive chair, Cook will still conduct some of Apple’s high-level policy duties, including the equivalent of stuffing gold-plated binkies in the presidential mouth. Ternus implies that the reality is more nuanced. “Tim is available to help wherever I ask him, and it's great to have him in that role,” he said. “He obviously has a ton of relationships he's developed over the years, and of course, I'm building new relationships in this role as well.” One relationship he has yet to build: the president. Ternus has yet to meet Donald Trump.

Then there’s the one thing that could possibly disrupt the way Apple has run its business for the past 50 years. Ternus is taking over the company during what may be the biggest technological shift ever. I suggested to Ternus that history may judge him on how he handles AI. I spelled out for him a couple of narratives people spin about Apple. One is that Apple has been hobbled by a failure to develop its AI product Siri, and even after an update it’s still in catch-up mode. The other is that Apple is smart to avoid the high cost of developing a frontier model and that the strategy of organically putting AI into its products, with a focus on privacy, will pay off in the long run.

“Everyone has an opinion—I really like where we’re at,” he said. “I would hope people recognize that the work we do is building incredible products that make their lives better. We’re absolutely going to leverage AI to do that. We don't want to ship AI for AI's sake. When we're doing it right, people won’t have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen or more traditional software. What matters is, did we build something that they really love?”

That assumes that AI, as powerful as it is, will wind up as a “normal” technology, organically integrated into our current gadget-sphere. Another school of thought is that AI is an apocalyptic disruptor that will shred the current ecosystem. In that vision, all those cool apps Apple supports will be subsumed by AI-concocted agents generated from prompts, or even autonomously. Ternus doesn’t buy that scenario. “That could make life really easy, I suppose, but the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing, something that we love to do,” he said.

When I asked whether he’s in favor of AI regulation, he replied, “We all read the stories and think about it from a cybersecurity standpoint—clearly these models are very capable of doing things. Our focus is on making sure that our products are secure and safe, and protecting the users' information.”

His non-answer shows that he might well be on the way to mastering political communication. But policy will never be the focus of John Ternus. He is, and probably always will be, the product-guy CEO. Before we ended our conversation, Ternus had one question for me: “What did you think of the logo?”

news.title_zh: 苹果新CEO谈AI战略与政商关系
news.summary_zh: 苹果现任CEO约翰·特纳斯在洛杉矶新品发布会上表示，苹果不会为了AI而做AI，并透露库克随时提供政策协助

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 苹果新任CEO约翰·特纳斯在洛杉矶举行的MacBook Pro新品低调发布会后接受媒体专访，针对外界关注的AI布局及宏观政策表态。他强调苹果绝不为了蹭热度而盲目推出AI功能，同时透露前CEO蒂姆·库克在其需要时会随时提供政策支持，而他本人目前尚未与特朗普会面。此次亮相旨在延续苹果务实的产品路线，向外界传递在AI时代硬件体验依然至上的信号。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Apple's new CEO John Ternus stated in an interview following a low-key product launch event in Los Angeles that Apple refuses to ship AI just for the sake of it. He also mentioned that Tim Cook remains available to assist with policy wherever needed, while noting he has yet to meet with Trump. The move aims to signal that hardware still rules supreme at Apple even in the age of AI.

news.article_content_zh:
本周推出新款 Macbook Pro 的简短仪式与主礼人苹果新任首席执行官 John Ternus 一样低调。他以零张扬的方式走上洛杉矶活动场地的低台，打了个招呼，然后排队观看了一段展示第一台触摸屏 Mac 的视频。然后，他放出了一小群记者和创作者，让他们亲身体验这款新笔记本电脑，并在音乐制作人、电影制作人、摄影师和时装设计师使用笔记本电脑进行令人眼花缭乱的演示之间漫游。特努斯现年 51 岁，是苹果高层管理人员中较为年轻的一员，他担任首席执行官还不到两个月。但这次发布和最近的一系列其他公告已经清楚地表明了一件事。对于这个新人来说——如果一个在苹果工作了 25 年的老员工可以被认为是新人的话——一切都与产品有关。也许恰如其分的是，当 Ternus 透露新设备恢复了苹果标志的照明时，演示中最大的噪音出现了。也许这象征着在人工智能时代，苹果正在传递硬件仍然占主导地位的信息。

演讲结束几分钟后，我与 Ternus 坐下来，这是两天内第二次。史蒂夫·乔布斯 (Steve Jobs) 也曾在他著名的主题演讲结束后邀请我来听。当然，特努斯不是乔布斯，他也不应该是乔布斯。但他是谁？

我第一次见到 Ternus 是在 2015 年，当时我在苹果的输入设计实验室（库比蒂诺的一个测试设施）和他一起度过了一天。他已升任 Mac、iPad、生态系统和音频工程副总裁，给我的印象是和蔼可亲、知识渊博。 （他大学毕业后在一家虚拟现实公司工作了四年，但从那时起他就一直在苹果工作。）当时我的故事的核心是，这位不知名的经理如何进行一项类似沙威的调查，以修复重新设计的鼠标在桌子上滑动时发出的奇怪声音。

对细节的关注是乔布斯完美主义的遗产，蒂姆·库克在担任下一任首席执行官时也继承了这一传统。在特纳斯与乔布斯重叠的十年里，他说自己与这位创始人只有“少量互动”。 “但我一直感觉自己像是史蒂夫教诲的学生，”特努斯说。 “能够与蒂姆密切合作，我非常幸运。”

到目前为止，Ternus 以其产品实力而闻名。苹果全球营销高级副总裁、在公司工作 40 年的资深人士格雷格·乔斯维亚克 (Greg Joswiak) 表示：“约翰天生对优秀产品有着敏锐的洞察力，而这正是苹果的本质。” “你不能教这个。”从某种意义上说，Ternus 的晋升与微软的萨蒂亚·纳德拉（Satya Nadella）类似，后者是另一位终身晋升到最高职位的人。但纳德拉被要求修复一个破碎的组织，而苹果已经持续了数十年。特努斯明确表示，他将成为连续性的引擎。这个词是他选择的关键，最重要的是解释了为什么蒂姆·库克和苹果董事会的其他成员对这个选择如此满意。

当我询问特努斯对成为公司领导者的看法时，他在苹果内部的地位就显而易见了。我问他欣赏哪些非苹果公司的首席执行官，他被难住了。 “我还没有真正考虑过这一点，”他说。我问是否有任何商业书籍对他产生了影响。 “不完全是，”他说。 “我当然读过书，但从与我共事的人身上可以学到很多东西。”事实上，每次我试图向特努斯明确他想在苹果公司留下什么印记时，他都会转移问题，并告诉我他将如何继续苹果公司对内部合作的承诺。

Ternus 的主要合作者可能是 Johny Srouji，他是该公司定制芯片的架构师，这一举措在过去十年推动了该公司的许多创新。 Srouri 表示，随着苹果公司将其硬件工程和技术组织与 Srouji 合并，他们的关系将会更加密切，并向 Ternus 汇报。 “约翰将成为一位伟大的首席执行官，”他说。 “他本质上是一个产品人，但苹果的秘密武器是 DNA、文化，这是不会改变的。记住，约翰已经在这里工作了 25 年。他不会来，一切都会不同。”

作为苹果公司的首席执行官，不仅仅涉及产品——还有价值 1000 亿美元的服务业务、庞大的基础设施以及运营一家大公司的普遍错误。我问 Ternus 大规模扩展投资组合是什么感觉。 “这份工作的一个令人惊奇的特权就是可以学到很多新东西，”他说。 “我一直并将继续学习并深入不同的领域。但是，你知道，我确实喜欢产品。我对此充满热情。”

不管你喜欢与否，一家价值 4 万亿美元的公司的首席执行官必须参与政策和政治。据广泛报道，作为执行主席，库克仍将履行苹果的一些高层政策职责，包括相当于在总统嘴里塞金币。 Ternus 暗示现实更加微妙。 “无论我向蒂姆提出什么要求，蒂姆都可以提供帮助，很高兴让他担任这个角色，”他说。 “显然，他多年来建立了很多关系，当然，我也在这个角色中建立新的关系。”他尚未建立一种关系：总统。特纳斯尚未会见唐纳德·特朗普。

还有一件事可能会颠覆苹果过去 50 年的业务运营方式。 Ternus 正在接管该公司，这可能是有史以来最大的技术变革。我向特努斯建议，历史可能会根据他处理人工智能的方式来评判他。我向他详细讲述了人们对苹果的一些叙述。一是苹果因人工智能产品Siri开发失败而陷入困境，即使更新后仍处于追赶状态。另一个原因是，苹果很聪明地避免了开发前沿模型的高成本，并且将人工智能有机地融入其产品中并注重隐私的战略从长远来看将获得回报。

“每个人都有自己的意见——我真的很喜欢我们现在的处境，”他说。 “我希望人们认识到，我们所做的工作是打造令人难以置信的产品，让他们的生活变得更美好。我们绝对会利用人工智能来做到这一点。我们不想为了人工智能而提供人工智能。当我们做得正确时，人们就不必考虑是人工智能还是更传统的软件实现了这一点。重要的是，我们是否构建了他们真正喜欢的东西？”

假设人工智能虽然强大，但最终将成为一种“正常”技术，有机地融入我们当前的小工具领域。另一种观点认为，人工智能是一种世界末日般的破坏者，将粉碎当前的生态系统。在这个愿景中，苹果支持的所有那些很酷的应用程序都将被包含在根据提示生成的人工智能代理中，甚至是自动生成的代理中。特纳斯并不相信这种情况。 “我认为，这可以让生活变得非常轻松，但产品的创造是一件非常人性化和个性化的事情，也是我们喜欢做的事情，”他说。

当我问他是否支持人工智能监管时，他回答说：“我们都读过这些故事，并从网络安全的角度思考——显然这些模型非常有能力做事。我们的重点是确保我们的产品安全可靠，并保护用户的信息。”

他的不回答表明他很可能正在掌握政治沟通的道路上。但政策永远不会成为约翰·特努斯的关注焦点。他现在是，而且很可能永远是，产品型首席执行官。在我们结束谈话之前，Ternus 问了我一个问题：“你觉得这个标志怎么样？”

news.title: Sources: OpenAI has secured ~$11B in commitments for its latest funding round, less than half its initial $30B target, and expects to raise more in coming weeks (Berber Jin/Wall Street Journal)
news.title_en: Sources: OpenAI has secured ~$11B in commitments for its latest funding round, less than half its initial $30B target, and expects to raise more in coming weeks (Berber Jin/Wall Street Journal)
news.author: Wall Street Journal
news.original_content:
Berber Jin / Wall Street Journal:
Sources: OpenAI has secured ~$11B in commitments for its latest funding round, less than half its initial $30B target, and expects to raise more in coming weeks  —  The ChatGPT maker's latest funding round values it at $1.25 trill
news.content_snippet: The ChatGPT maker's latest funding round values it at $1.25 trillion, less than its $1.4 trillion target
news.summary_en: OpenAI has secured approximately $11 billion in commitments for its latest funding round, falling well short of its initial $30 billion ambition. Under immense pressure from soaring compute bills and model development costs, the company expects to raise additional capital from investors over the coming weeks.
news.title_zh: OpenAI新轮融资获百亿美元承诺 不及最初目标一半
news.summary_zh: OpenAI最新一轮融资已锁定约110亿美元出资承诺，虽远低于300亿美元初始目标，但数周内还将继续筹资

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: OpenAI在最新一轮融资中已获得约110亿美元的出资承诺，目前仅达成其最初300亿美元募资目标的三分之一左右。随着大模型研发与前沿算力成本持续呈指数级飙升，OpenAI正面临极为沉重的烧钱压力，预计将在未来数周内继续吸纳更多资本以充实弹药库。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: OpenAI has secured approximately $11 billion in commitments for its latest funding round, falling well short of its initial $30 billion ambition. Under immense pressure from soaring compute bills and model development costs, the company expects to raise additional capital from investors over the coming weeks.

elements_en.what: Secured ~$11B in commitments against a $30B target, with further fundraising ongoing
elements_en.why: Escalating compute infrastructure expenditures and model development costs requiring massive liquidity

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 原打算大笔一挥化缘300亿，结果金主爸爸们的钱包也扛不住这无底洞式的消耗。110亿美元放在任何行业都是天文数字，但在奥特曼每天如流水般的算力账单面前，也不过是够烧几个季度的柴火——华尔街和硅谷显然也开始对'无限烧钱换AGI'的故事稍作冷静了。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Aiming for $30 billion and walking away with $11 billion shows that even the deepest venture pockets are blinking at AI's bottomless burn rate. Eleven billion is staggering by any normal standard, but against Sam Altman's compute bills, it's merely a few quarters' worth of firewood before the collection plate passes around again.

news.title: Sources: Baseten is raising ~$2B in two tranches, one valuing it at $26B and the other at $30B; Baseten was valued at $13B in June after raising $1.5B (Bloomberg)
news.title_en: Sources: Baseten is raising ~$2B in two tranches, one valuing it at $26B and the other at $30B; Baseten was valued at $13B in June after raising $1.5B (Bloomberg)
news.author: Bloomberg
news.original_content:
Bloomberg:
Sources: Baseten is raising ~$2B in two tranches, one valuing it at $26B and the other at $30B; Baseten was valued at $13B in June after raising $1.5B  —  Artificial intelligence startup Baseten is set to raise new funding that would more than double it
news.content_snippet: Artificial intelligence startup Baseten is set to raise new funding that would more than double its valuation to about $30 billion, according to people familiar with the efforts.
news.summary_en: Artificial intelligence startup Baseten is preparing to raise approximately $2 billion in two tranches, valuing the company at $26 billion and $30 billion respectively. Having reached a $13 billion valuation in June following a $1.5 billion funding round, this planned transaction will more than double its valuation within months. The aggressive round highlights massive investor appetite for underlying AI inference and deployment infrastructure amid soaring enterprise workload demands.
news.title_zh: 人工智能独角兽拟分批融资20亿美元 估值半年飙至300亿
news.summary_zh: 人工智能初创企业Baseten正筹划两批次总计约20亿美元的新一轮融资，最新估值最高将达到300亿美元

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 人工智能初创公司Baseten正计划分两批次筹集约20亿美元的新资金，第一批次估值为260亿美元，第二批次估值将进一步推升至300亿美元。该公司在今年6月刚完成15亿美元融资并斩获130亿美元估值，此次动作意味着其身价在短短半年内再度翻倍。这一激进融资反映出企业级模型推理与算力部署需求暴涨背景下，一级市场对底层AI基础设施服务商的极度渴求。

ai_analysis.insight_en: Bagging a $13 billion valuation just six months ago and now demanding up to $30 billion proves AI valuation inflation outpaces any central bank printer. VCs publicly fret about compute bubbles while quietly queueing up for tiered markup rounds, terrified of missing the next inference landlord. At this stage, writing these checks isn't financial underwriting—it's paying pure ransom for scarce AI compute exposure.

news.original_content:
Bloomberg:
Sources: Google is in talks with the DOD on a new effort to secure the data that feeds into software being built for the Golden Dome missile defense program  —  Alphabet Inc.'s Google is in talks with the US Defense Department to work on a new data secu
news.content_snippet: Alphabet Inc.'s Google is in talks with the US Defense Department to work on a new data security effort underpinning …
news.summary_en: Google is currently in discussions with the US Department of Defense to secure data feeding into software under development for the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. The partnership focuses on safeguarding mission-critical data streams against tampering within strategic interception infrastructures. The move highlights the Pentagon's rigorous cybersecurity requirements and Google's escalating ambition to capture lucrative defense contracts.

The move highlights the Pentagon's rigorous cybersecurity requirements and Google's escalating ambition to capture lucrative defense contracts.

news.title: How a Contractor’s Claude Agent Got Into the Pentagon
news.title_en: How a Contractor’s Claude Agent Got Into the Pentagon
news.author: Wired AI
news.article_content:
This week on Uncanny Valley, Brian Barrett, Leah Feiger, and Zoë Schiffer dive into our scoop on how a defense contractor connected Claude Code to a secure Department of Defense system. We also discuss the green, yellow, and red flags we see in Anthropic’s IPO filing—and why it’s a test not just for the AI industry, but for the entire US economy—and how volunteers nationwide are preparing for ICE agents potentially showing up at polling sites in the midterms.

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Welcome to the WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Zoë Schiffer: I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Zoë Schiffer: This week, Anthropic has officially filed to go public. There is a lot going on in the hundreds of pages that the company submitted as part of its S-1 filing, from staggering earnings and losses, to warnings of AI's existential threat. Obviously, we're talking about Anthropic here. We'll discuss our key takeaways and why this IPO is kind of high stakes, not just for the AI industry, but honestly the entire US economy.

Leah Feiger: We're also bringing you a scoop about how a defense contractor plugged Anthropic's Claude into a secure Department of Defense system, in what's really one of the most outlandish uses of AI in the government we've seen so far.

Brian Barrett: And the midterms are right around the corner, just a few days away. Massive groups of volunteers all over the country are already getting ready to protect their communities from the potential that ICE officers show up at the polls. We'll get into how grassroots efforts like these are a reflection of a deeply uncertain election cycle.

Zoë Schiffer: So on Monday, we learned that Anthropic finally pulled the trigger and publicly filed for its IPO. This has been highly anticipated for a bunch of reasons. Anthropic is expected to raise more money in its IPO than any company in history, and it would be the first major US company focused solely on building AI software to go public. To give you a sense of the scale that we're talking about, the company's valuation went from $183 billion a little over a year ago to $965 billion in its most recent round, and some expect that it could be worth close to $2 trillion once it starts trading. So the filing basically gives us the first real look inside Anthropic's business because it's a private company right now. It doesn't have to report a bunch of stuff. And the numbers are pretty extreme in both directions, billions of dollars in revenue and even more billions in losses, and hundreds of billions that the company has already committed to compute. Because there's a ton to unpack in this paperwork, I thought it would be fun to divide it into green flags, yellow flags, and red flags that we saw from the filing. What do you guys think?

Leah Feiger: I'm astounded by how much money is at play here. This is, yes.

Brian Barrett: What flag, Leah? What flag is that?

Zoë Schiffer: For the sake of the economy, it's green.

Leah Feiger: For the sake of the economy, it's green. This is so much money, guys. Sue me, but the only thing I can think of right now is that article that WIRED ran a couple of months ago about how people were selling their homes in the Bay Area with the promise of Anthropic stock post-IPO. And I remember at the time I was like, "How close are we to this?" And Zoe said, "Oh, they're going to make so much money."

Brian Barrett: Is it fair to say, Zoë, I feel like having the financials out there, yes, they're losing money hand over fist, but the financials I think are better than people were expecting maybe. At least, it feels like they put a lot of concerns to rest, not all of them, but this is a real business. This is a business that is growing. It's doing all the things you would want a business to do.

Zoë Schiffer: Yes, I think absolutely. So its revenue hit $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, and it's grown more than 14 fold from the same period last year. I think we have to go back to 2022 and remember that when ChatGPT came on the scene, it wasn't even apparent that AI would have a real enterprise application. This was a consumer app that didn't have really any business case for it. And it wasn't until Anthropic came on the scene years later, it rolled out Claude Code that we started to really see like, oh no, there's a viable business and actually the majority of the money is going to come from other businesses using their coding product. This is also, I think, a key difference that you hear from insiders between Dario and Sam. People very close to Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, will say he wakes up every single day and says, "Enterprise code." That is the thing he cares about. And that's because that's the thing that makes money for these businesses. Whereas I think the perception from some is that OpenAI is a little more scattered and all over the place. And I think you can see that in the numbers.

Brian Barrett: So they are leaning in. They have Claude code, huge success, enterprise code, huge success. Leah Feiger：我对这里的资金投入感到惊讶。这是，是的。

布莱恩·巴雷特：莉亚，什么旗子？那是什么旗？

Zoë Schiffer：为了经济，它是绿色的。

Leah Feiger：为了经济，它是绿色的。这是这么多钱，伙计们。告我吧，但我现在唯一能想到的就是《连线》几个月前发表的那篇文章，内容是关于人们如何在首次公开募股后承诺 Anthropic 股票的情况下出售湾区的房屋。我记得当时我就想，“我们离这个目标还有多远？”佐伊说：“哦，他们会赚很多钱的。”

布莱恩·巴雷特：公平地说，佐伊，我想把财务状况公布出来，是的，他们正在大量亏损，但我认为财务状况可能比人们预期的要好。至少，感觉他们消除了很多担忧，不是全部，但这是一桩真正的生意。这是一项正在增长的业务。它正在做您希望企业做的所有事情。

Zoë Schiffer：是的，我认为绝对如此。因此，2026 年上半年其收入达到 163 亿美元，比去年同期增长了 14 倍多。我认为我们必须回到 2022 年并记住，当 ChatGPT 出现时，人工智能是否会拥有真正的企业应用程序甚至还不是很明显。这是一款消费者应用程序，实际上没有任何商业案例。直到几年后 Anthropic 出现，它推出了 Claude Code，我们才开始真正看到，哦不，这是一个可行的业务，实际上大部分资金将来自使用其编码产品的其他企业。我认为，这也是您从内部人士那里听到的达里奥和萨姆之间的一个关键区别。与 Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 关系密切的人会说，他每天醒来都会说“企业代码”。这才是他关心的事情。那是因为这就是这些企业赚钱的东西。但我认为有些人的看法是 OpenAI 更加分散且遍布各个地方。我想你可以从数字中看到这一点。

Brian Barrett：所以他们正在努力。他们有 Claude Code，取得了巨大的成功，企业代码，取得了巨大的成功。我要说的是，举个黄旗，在你谈到的收入中，令人印象深刻的收入超过 600 亿美元，其中近一半来自三个科技公司的云市场。因此，他们非常依赖少数同时也是竞争对手的公司。正是这个行业中这种错综复杂的依赖巢穴让人感觉，我认为 Anthropic 并没有把它作为其主要风险因素之一。我们可以立即讨论风险因素，因为那是我最喜欢的部分，但它确实让人感觉，护城河在哪里？考虑到他们对少数几家也在开发自己的人工智能的公司的依赖程度是否足够，其他人工智能产品正在变得更好，开源产品、开放权重产品都在那里。那面旗帜有多黄？

Zoë Schiffer：我认为它是黄色的。一个多角恋工人合作社在商业交易中出现乱伦也就不足为奇了。我对这个信息并不感到震惊。一小部分消费者对公司收入产生巨大影响的情况并不罕见。我认为 Ramp 最近发布的另一个数字是，Anthropic 和 OpenAI 80% 的收入来自大约 1% 的 AI 消费者。因此，支出最多的公司占公司收入的绝大多数。但这是一个漏洞，因为如果出现回调并且这些公司开始减少支出，Anthropic 就会受到影响。但另一个，我不知道该把这个标志放在哪里。我认为它是绿色的。他们对 IPO 涉及的一些风险以及人工智能普遍存在的一些风险保持透明。这可能是整个事情中我最喜欢的部分。 “人们担心......足够先进的人工智能系统如果没有得到适当的开发和保护，可能会给人类带来灾难性或生存风险。”

Zoë Schiffer：达里奥（Dario）对 S-1 中被动语态的使用提出了担忧，认为这是真的。

Brian Barrett：在 Anthropic 内部，我也会说，“存在风险”一词出现了三次。这是对人类的两倍的生存风险，一次对社会的生存风险。因此，在这种情况下，大概仍然有人类，他们只是放弃了任何社会契约的形式。

Brian Barrett：需要明确的是，自从他们开始以来，他们就一直在喊话人工智能可以杀死所有人。这对他们来说并不新鲜。我认为很有趣，我将其称为红旗，人类的红旗，人类的黄旗，我的绿旗，因为我喜欢谈论它。因此，他们认为最有可能导致地球上人类生命终结的事情，也是他们的主要竞争优势之一。这就是递归的自我完善。这就是人工智能模型可以自我改进的地方。一方面，他们说，如果人工智能模型不断改进自己，最终能够改进到人类甚至不需要看它的程度，关闭人工智能变得更好的循环，让人工智能变得更好，让人工智能变得更好，让我们甚至不明白人工智能在做什么，但是天哪，它很好，而且赚了很多钱，这就是人工智能强大到足以终结世界的场景。但 Anthropic 也指出，我们也非常擅长这一点。我们在这方面投入了大量资金。这就是我们取得进步的方式。

Zoë Schiffer：这有多相关？我们当中谁没有阴影面，而阴影面赋予你的力量同样增强了它？

Leah Feiger：需要明确的是，《连线》杂志报道了这一点，基本上每个人都报道了这一点。当前 Anthropic 研究员 Jacob Coxon 辞职并表示这是因为 Anthropic 可能带来世界末日时，他特别将遏制 RSI 列为首要任务。这就是整个球赛。

布莱恩·巴雷特：是的。然后整个行业非常......我认为这可能太极端了，但是伯尼·桑德斯有一项法案，罗·卡纳有一项单独的法案说：“嘿，让我们禁止递归自我改进。让我们说我们不会这样做。”我要说的一点是，风险因素是招股说明书中最长的部分。我相信它有 94 页。所以他们可以直接说：“我们有阴影面，拯救了所有人。

Leah Feiger：我们能谈谈一个危险信号吗？我还没有得到很好的答案，我需要你像个小孩一样向我解释一下？计算费用，所有这些技术都要花费很多钱。我个人并不觉得我了解限制在哪里，如何花足够的钱来使用你所有的钱，同时也花足够的钱来不让自己破产并永远结束你的技术。也许我不完全理解计算或它从何而来，但所有这些加在一起，就这么多了。告诉我。

佐伊·希弗：太多了。我不会假装我理解它。我们所讨论的规模再次是前所未有的。当你开始谈论这些东西时，你会得到很多铁路类比，但我想说，一个关键的区别是，与利润率略低的铁路公司不同，这些公司仍然是资金雄厚且富有的公司。是的，他们在计算方面投入了大量资金，并且他们预计将需要这种计算。到目前为止，他们预计这一数字将继续上升。我个人认为这是一个可行的论点，但当然，另一面是，如果增长开始严重放缓，他们将承担他们所承诺的所有计算的费用，以及 Anthropic 签署的许多合同，他们无法摆脱。这将非常糟糕，不仅对 Anthropic 不利，而且对整个美国经济也不利。

Leah Feiger：在报价中，他们称其为最重要的运营成本。

Brian Barrett：我认为也很重要，与 SpaceX、Meta 等其他在人工智能领域投入巨资的公司不同，Anthropic 所做的很多事情基本上都是租赁计算。他们没有建造那么多。他们正在外包。因此，一方面，这可能使他们摆脱对这些巨大财产的长期义务。另一方面，显然，在佐伊看来，他们是无法摆脱的合同。他们致力于这些合同，但在这方面他们并不能真正控制自己的命运，尤其是在现在计算竞争非常激烈的情况下。获得计算能力真的非常非常困难。这变得越来越困难，特别是当金融公司不太愿意提供债务、支持债务来支付所有这些基础设施成本时。我想很快补充的一件事是，他们在招股说明书中确实说，我只需要指出这一点，公司需要进行远期投资，这些投资一开始看起来是“不负责任的大”，如果 Zoë 发现影子是自我相关的，我发现这一点是相关的，因为这是我每次订购 DoorDash 时告诉我的家人的事情。

Brian Barrett：乍一看，它会大得不负责任。

Leah Feiger：首先，我想详细了解这些细节，每个人都应该在wired.com 上阅读本文，但我认为我真正想在这里传达的最重要的事情是我们以前从未见过这一点。这是一个巨大的例子，人工智能代理在理论上会造成严重破坏，甚至在人们不知情的情况下访问政府系统。

Brian Barrett：首先，Tori 的独家独家新闻。主要归功于她。真的，真的做得很好。我很惊讶没有一个系统可以捕捉到这一点。我很惊讶这种事一开始就被允许发生。感觉这里存在多个层面的失败，我认为国防部就说明了这一点，我认为这种情况正在各种组织中发生，因为人们变得更加依赖代理为他们做任何事情。

佐伊·希弗：是的。天哪，那些人。利亚，我想问你的问题是，我们不知道正在发生任何邪恶的事情。该承包商试图使用 Claude 来编写代码并进行部署。

利亚·费格：是的。所以这并不是一次大规模的黑客攻击。

Zoë Schiffer：我认为这更有趣。
